courses.name: Data Structures & Algorithms
courses.curriculum_text: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs; asymptotic (Big-O, Big-Theta) analysis of time and space; recursion and divide-and-conquer; sorting algorithms (insertion, quicksort, mergesort, heapsort, counting sort) and their tradeoffs; hash tables, hash function design, and collision handling by chaining and open addressing; binary search trees and balanced trees (AVL, red-black); heaps and priority queues; graph representations, traversal (BFS/DFS), topological sort, shortest paths (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford), and minimum spanning trees (Kruskal, Prim); greedy algorithms and exchange arguments; dynamic programming over sequences, grids, and subsets, with memoization and tabulation; union-find with path compression; amortized analysis; string matching; an introduction to NP-completeness and reductions. Weekly problem sets are implemented in a systems language and graded on both correctness and measured complexity. Students finish able to pick a data structure from a problem statement and defend the choice.

curriculum_variants.label: Competitive Programming Track
curriculum_variants.text: A faster-paced version built around contest-style problem solving: the same core structures (arrays, trees, graphs, heaps) but reached quickly so most of the term is spent on timed problem sets modeled on ICPC/Codeforces rounds — two-pointer and sliding-window techniques, bitmasking, segment trees and Fenwick trees, advanced graph algorithms (SCCs, articulation points, LCA), number theory for programming, and contest-speed implementation under a clock. Formal proofs of correctness are covered briefly; the emphasis is recognizing which structure a problem wants and implementing it fast and bug-free. Grading is mostly live contest scores plus a handful of harder take-home problems.

courses.name: Object-Oriented Programming
courses.curriculum_text: Classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance, composition, and polymorphism; interfaces and abstract classes; static and dynamic dispatch; generics and type parameters; design patterns (factory, builder, observer, strategy, decorator, adapter, singleton) and when each is the wrong choice; UML class, sequence, and state diagrams; the SOLID principles and dependency inversion; refactoring toward smaller objects; unit testing, test doubles, and test-driven development; exception handling and error-signalling strategy; object lifecycle, copy semantics, and basic memory management including garbage collection and reference counting; equality, hashing, and immutability contracts; package structure and API design for reuse. A semester-long team project builds a mid-sized application from a written requirement using a shared repository, branch-per-feature version control, and peer code review; grading covers design quality and test coverage, not only working output. Weekly labs convert procedural code into an object model and argue the tradeoff.

curriculum_variants.label: Systems Design Track
curriculum_variants.text: Covers the same OOP fundamentals (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces) but spends the back half of the course on how those ideas scale into larger systems: module boundaries and dependency graphs, service decomposition, event-driven vs. request-driven object collaboration, and the tradeoffs between inheritance-heavy and composition-heavy designs in a real multi-package codebase. Design patterns are taught by refactoring an existing messy application rather than from a catalog. The team project builds a plugin-style system where independent teams' modules must interoperate through an agreed interface, graded partly on how well the boundary held up under a late requirement change.

courses.name: Database Management Systems
courses.curriculum_text: Relational model and relational algebra; ER modeling and schema design; SQL in depth — joins, subqueries, set operations, aggregation, grouping, and window functions; views and common table expressions; normalization from 1NF to BCNF and the cases for deliberate denormalization; physical storage, B-tree and hash indexing, and reading query execution plans; the basics of query optimization, cardinality estimation, and join ordering; transactions, the ACID properties, isolation levels, and the anomalies each permits; concurrency control by two-phase locking and multiversion concurrency control; deadlock handling; write-ahead logging, recovery, and backups; stored procedures and triggers; an introduction to document, key-value, and column stores, and when to reach for them instead. A semester project designs a multi-table schema from a domain description, loads realistic data, and tunes a set of slow queries with indexes and rewrites; students present before-and-after execution plans.

curriculum_variants.label: Applied Data Engineering Track
curriculum_variants.text: The same relational foundations (schema design, SQL, indexing, transactions) but oriented toward moving and shaping data rather than serving an app: batch and streaming ETL patterns, staging/warehouse layer design, partitioning and clustering for analytical queries, slowly-changing dimensions, idempotent pipeline design, and data quality checks. Less time on formal normal-form proofs; more on when a denormalized analytics table is the right call. Labs use a real orchestration tool to build a multi-stage pipeline from raw source tables to a query-ready warehouse schema, with a focus on making failed runs re-runnable without duplicating data.

courses.name: Operating Systems
courses.curriculum_text: Process and thread models, context switching, and the process lifecycle; CPU scheduling (round-robin, priority, multilevel feedback, completely fair) and how each starves; synchronization primitives — mutexes, semaphores, condition variables, and barriers — applied to the classic concurrency problems; race conditions, atomicity, and memory visibility; deadlock detection, prevention, and avoidance; virtual memory, paging, page-replacement policies, and thrashing; memory allocators; file system layout, inodes, journalling, and I/O scheduling; buffering and caching; interprocess communication by pipes, shared memory, signals, and sockets; system calls and the user/kernel boundary; interrupts and device drivers; an introduction to virtualization and containers. Labs are written in C against a Unix-like kernel: a shell with job control, a thread-safe allocator, a producer-consumer pipeline, and a user-level thread scheduler. Debugging with gdb, strace, and valgrind is examined.

curriculum_variants.label: Kernel Internals Track
curriculum_variants.text: Covers the same process/thread, scheduling, and memory fundamentals but through direct reading of Linux kernel source rather than a textbook model: the actual scheduler implementation, the page allocator, the VFS layer, and how system calls are dispatched. Labs replace the from-scratch shell/allocator assignments with kernel-adjacent work — writing a loadable kernel module, instrumenting scheduler behavior with tracepoints, and patching a small kernel subsystem. Less time on abstract deadlock proofs; more time reading and modifying real, messy production-grade C. Assumes comfort with C and a Unix environment coming in.

courses.name: Computer Networks
courses.curriculum_text: The OSI and TCP/IP layering models and the end-to-end argument; the physical and link layers, framing, error detection, Ethernet, and switching; IP addressing, subnetting, CIDR, NAT, and IPv6; intra- and inter-domain routing (link-state, distance-vector, and BGP at a high level); the transport layer in depth — UDP, TCP connection setup and teardown, reliable delivery, flow control, and congestion control (slow start, AIMD, and modern variants); the application layer — HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, DNS resolution, TLS handshakes, email and file-transfer protocols; socket programming and the client-server model; network security fundamentals including certificates, firewalls, and common attacks; an introduction to distributed-systems tradeoffs of latency, partition tolerance, and consistency. Labs build a concurrent client-server application over raw sockets and a reliable-transfer protocol on top of UDP, and require capturing and explaining real traffic in a packet analyser.

curriculum_variants.label: Applied Infrastructure Track
curriculum_variants.text: The same layered networking model and transport/application-layer fundamentals, reoriented toward operating networks rather than just understanding them: cloud VPC design, subnetting in practice, load balancers and reverse proxies, service discovery, DNS-based routing, TLS termination, and debugging real latency and packet-loss issues with production tooling. BGP and inter-domain routing are covered at a survey level rather than in depth. Labs stand up a small multi-service application behind a load balancer and a CDN, then deliberately break it (packet loss, a misconfigured proxy, a certificate issue) for the student to diagnose.

courses.name: Machine Learning
courses.curriculum_text: Supervised learning: linear and logistic regression, regularized variants, k-nearest neighbours, naive Bayes, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, and support vector machines with kernels; unsupervised learning: k-means and hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering, PCA and dimensionality reduction; model evaluation — train/validation/test splits, k-fold cross-validation, precision, recall, F1, ROC and precision-recall curves, confusion matrices, and choosing a metric for imbalanced data; feature engineering, encoding, scaling, and feature selection; the bias-variance tradeoff, overfitting, and learning curves; hyperparameter search; loss functions, gradient descent and its variants, and an introduction to feedforward neural networks and backpropagation; the linear algebra, calculus, and probability the above rests on; data leakage and reproducibility. Coursework is in Python with standard numerical and ML libraries; a final project trains, tunes, and evaluates a model on a real dataset and reports honest error analysis.

curriculum_variants.label: Deep Learning Track
curriculum_variants.text: Classical supervised/unsupervised methods are covered at survey depth in the first few weeks; most of the course is neural networks: feedforward nets and backpropagation from scratch, convolutional and recurrent architectures, optimization tricks (batch norm, dropout, learning-rate schedules), transfer learning from pretrained models, and an introduction to attention and transformers. Evaluation methodology (splits, cross-validation, metric choice) is still covered, just applied to deep models instead of classical ones. The final project fine-tunes a pretrained model on a real dataset rather than training a classical model from scratch, and reports on what did and didn't transfer.

courses.name: Web Development
courses.curriculum_text: HTTP fundamentals — methods, status codes, headers, cookies, caching, and the request/response cycle; client-server architecture and the same-origin policy with CORS; designing and building REST APIs: routing, request validation, pagination, error contracts, versioning, and authentication with sessions and tokens; server-side data access and connecting an API to a relational database; frontend implementation with a component-based framework — components, props, state, effects, and lists; client-side state management and data fetching; forms, validation, and accessibility basics; responsive layout with modern CSS, flexbox, and grid; asset bundling and build tooling; environment configuration and secret handling; deployment of a two-service application, logging, and basic observability; an introduction to web security (XSS, CSRF, injection) and to WebSockets for live updates. A semester project ships a full-stack CRUD application with a real database, deployed to a public URL and reviewed on both API design and interface quality.

curriculum_variants.label: Full-Stack Product Track
curriculum_variants.text: Same HTTP/REST/auth fundamentals, taught against one specific modern stack (TypeScript, a component-based frontend framework, a Node-based API) instead of framework-agnostic examples, with more time on product concerns: optimistic UI updates, form state and validation libraries, component design systems, and shipping incremental features to a live deployment throughout the term rather than only at the end. Security and WebSockets are covered at the same depth. The semester project is scoped and re-scoped like a real product backlog — priorities shift partway through — and is graded partly on how cleanly the codebase absorbed the change.

courses.name: Software Engineering
courses.curriculum_text: The software development lifecycle and its common process models; eliciting, writing, and prioritising requirements, user stories, and acceptance criteria; estimation and planning; software architecture — layering, modularity, coupling and cohesion, architectural patterns, and documenting a design with diagrams and decision records; design patterns in the large; version control workflows, trunk-based development and branch-per-feature, code review practice, and merge strategy; testing at every level — unit, integration, contract, system, and regression — plus coverage, test doubles, and flaky-test triage; continuous integration and continuous delivery pipelines, build reproducibility, and release management; agile practice: sprints, standups, backlog grooming, retrospectives, and velocity; technical debt, refactoring, and legacy-code strategy; defect tracking, incident response, and postmortems; software licensing and professional ethics. A semester-long team project runs as real sprints against a genuine external stakeholder, with a working increment demonstrated at the end of each iteration.

curriculum_variants.label: Startup / Lean Track
curriculum_variants.text: Covers the same lifecycle, testing, and CI/CD fundamentals but through a small-team, move-fast lens: lightweight requirements capture (no heavy documents), rapid prototyping and throwaway code as a deliberate tool, minimum-viable architecture, and deciding what not to build yet. Formal process (detailed decision records, heavyweight estimation ceremonies) is covered but framed as something a team graduates into as it grows, not a default. The semester project is scoped like an early-stage startup — a small team, a real but narrow problem, weekly demos to a stand-in founder, and explicit permission to cut corners the team can defend.

courses.name: Probability & Statistics
courses.curriculum_text: Probability axioms, sample spaces, combinatorics, conditional probability, independence, and Bayes' theorem; discrete and continuous random variables; the binomial, geometric, Poisson, uniform, exponential, and normal distributions and where each arises; joint, marginal, and conditional distributions; expectation, variance, covariance, and correlation; transformations and sums of random variables; the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem; sampling distributions; point estimation, maximum likelihood, bias, and standard error; confidence intervals; hypothesis testing, p-values, type I and type II error, power, and multiple-comparison correction; t-tests, chi-square tests, and ANOVA; simple and multiple linear regression, residual diagnostics, and interpretation of coefficients; the design and analysis of A/B tests, including sample-size calculation and common pitfalls; an introduction to Bayesian inference. Problem sets pair hand calculation with statistical software, and a final assignment analyses a real dataset and defends its conclusions.

curriculum_variants.label: Applied Data Science Track
curriculum_variants.text: The same distributions, estimation, and hypothesis-testing foundations, taught computationally rather than by hand: simulation-based intuition for the central limit theorem and confidence intervals, bootstrap and permutation tests alongside the classical parametric ones, and every technique immediately applied to a real dataset in code rather than proved on paper first. A/B testing gets more time, including sequential testing pitfalls and multiple-comparison correction in a real experimentation-platform context. The final project runs a full analysis pipeline — cleaning, exploratory analysis, a designed test, and a written recommendation — rather than a single hand-derived proof set.

courses.name: Computer Vision
courses.curriculum_text: Image formation, camera models, projection, and digital image representation; colour spaces and histograms; point operations, filtering, convolution, and frequency-domain analysis; noise models and denoising; edge detection (Sobel, Canny), corner and blob detection, and local feature descriptors with matching; image pyramids and scale space; segmentation by thresholding, clustering, region growing, and graph cuts; morphological operations; classical object detection and recognition with sliding windows and hand-crafted features; convolutional neural networks for classification, detection, and semantic segmentation, including transfer learning from pretrained backbones; data augmentation, labelling strategy, and dataset bias; camera calibration, homographies, stereo correspondence, depth estimation, and basic structure from motion; optical flow and tracking across frames; evaluation metrics such as IoU and mean average precision. A final project curates an image dataset, trains a vision model, and reports quantitative results with failure-case analysis.

curriculum_variants.label: Applied Deep Learning for Vision Track
curriculum_variants.text: Classical filtering, edge/corner detection, and hand-crafted features are covered briefly as historical context; most of the course is modern deep-learning vision: CNN architectures for classification/detection/segmentation, transfer learning from large pretrained backbones, data augmentation and labeling-pipeline design, and an introduction to vision transformers. Camera geometry and stereo are covered at survey depth rather than in full derivation. The final project fine-tunes and deploys a pretrained detection or segmentation model against a self-collected dataset, with the write-up focused on failure-case analysis and dataset bias rather than deriving the underlying math.
